title: Watchful, not anxious
hookLine: live each day ready and unafraid

lines: THE MASTER IS AT A WEDDING.
cards: It's late. The house is quiet, but nobody's gone to bed. Lamps still lit, belts still fastened, shoes still on.
The master of the house is at a wedding feast, and nobody knows when he'll be back. Midnight. Later.
Toward morning. The servants aren't pacing or panicking. They're just awake, with the door within reach, so that the moment he knocks, it opens.
Jesus tells this little scene in Luke's Gospel, and then adds a twist so strange it's easy to read right past it.

teach.b: First, the instruction: "Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning." Dressed for action, lamp lit. In Mark, Jesus puts it in one word, and widens it: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch."

The Greek word behind watch means stay awake. Second, the twist. When the master gets home and finds them awake, "he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them."
The master serves the servants. The one they've waited for waits on them. So watching isn't guarding against a punishment; it's staying up for someone who is coming home to feed you.
Third, not anxious. The same Jesus says, "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself."
And Paul writes, "Be careful for nothing." In the King James, careful means full of care, anxious, not cautious. Anxiety stares at tomorrow.
Watchfulness pays attention to now. Fourth, watching up close. In Gethsemane, Jesus takes three disciples a little way with him, asks them to watch with him, and goes on to pray.

teach.h: COULD YE NOT WATCH ONE HOUR?
teach.b: He comes back and finds them asleep: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" Then: "the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." Watching there isn't scanning the horizon.
It's staying with someone, awake, in the hour that's here. Readiness, in these stories, is attention to now, and the good in front of you, done well.

how: Churches that keep Advent watch toward Christ's coming in that season, and in vigils and night prayers; Gospel stories of watchful servants are among its readings.

o: keeping a strict eye on other people's faults
awake and ready, lamp lit, for someone coming home
anxious and on guard against a coming punishment

p: the master home from the wedding

s: in the King James, "be careful for nothing" means be careless
careful there means full of care, anxious. Paul is saying: don't be anxious.
in Luke's story, the master serves the servants who stayed awake
"he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them."
in Gethsemane, the disciples stayed awake with Jesus
he found them asleep: "what, could ye not watch with me one hour?"

games.q: you're the master, home late from a wedding. you knock, and your servants open at once, lamps lit. what do you do?
o: inspect the house for anything left undone.
put on an apron, sit them down and serve them.
send them to bed and eat alone.
games.why: "he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them." the one they waited for waits on them.

practice: Notice if your mind is running ahead, to tomorrow, next month, the end of everything, and let it come back to this day. Ask what ordinary good is in front of you: a meal to cook, a kid to pick up, a call to return.
If you pray, offer it to God as the thing you'd like to be found doing; if you don't, simply hold it with care.

wordCard.voice: Watchful. Awake and ready, lamp lit, for someone coming home. In the Gospels, it means doing today's good, without anxiety about tomorrow.

orig.note: Greek: watch, stay awake, Jesus's word in Mark 13:37.

carryVoice: Your line: ready, not afraid. Like servants awake for someone coming home. Rest well.
